html:
The Ibadis are followers of Ibadism, a branch of Islam distinct from both Sunni and Shia, which grew out of the early Kharijite movement but rejected its violence. On this map in 1200 they hold a stretch of the northern Sahara in Algeria, around the M'zab valley and Ouargla.

Ibadi missionaries from Basra spread the faith among Berbers in the 8th century. In North Africa they founded the Rustamid imamate, with its capital at Tahert, which ruled from 777 to 909. When the Fatimids destroyed Tahert, many Ibadis withdrew south to Sedrata near Ouargla, and from the 11th century to the M'zab valley.

There they built a cluster of walled towns, among them Ghardaïa, packed onto hilltops around a mosque, and farmed oases fed by deep wells. Strict community councils ran daily life. The Mzab towns still stand and are Ibadi today. The other great Ibadi land is Oman, beyond ancient Mascat.
